screens.title: The State Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we explore the State pattern and why it matters. Many objects change how they behave depending on internal conditions, and code that keeps checking those conditions quickly becomes brittle and hard to extend. The State pattern solves that by moving each state’s behavior into its own class. You’ll learn the three core parts — a Context that delegates behavior, a State interface defining the contract, and ConcreteState implementations that encapsulate behavior and transitions. We will see concrete Java examples such as a traffic light and a door, and you will practice implementing a MediaPlayer with Playing, Paused, and Stopped states. By the end you should be able to recognize when a large switch or many if-else branches really mean an opportunity for State, and you will be able to refactor to make code easier to extend without changing existing classes. Notice too how the State pattern differs from Strategy: State objects often drive transitions and know the context, while strategies are chosen externally and are usually stateless. Think about a traffic light changing from red to green as an object that appears to change its class, and ask yourself where you still rely on conditional switches in your own code.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › The State Pattern
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Terminal-first live coding feel · refactor demo

The State Pattern

Use state objects to localize behavior and transitions. Instead of checking internal flags with long conditionals, the context delegates to a state object that implements a common interface.

Problem
Large if-else or switch statements that handle behavior for many states.
Solution
Encapsulate behaviors in ConcreteState classes and let Context delegate.
Benefit
Easier extension and adherence to the Open/Closed Principle.
Key Takeaway

When behavior depends on internal state, move the behavior into state classes so adding states doesn't require changing core logic.

In this lesson
TrafficLight example
Red, Yellow, Green as separate state classes
Door example
Open, Closed, Locked behaviors
Hands-on
Starter code for MediaPlayer states
Coming up
A step-by-step refactor, code examples, common pitfalls, and a short assessment scenario you can try on your own.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will do four concrete tasks that show mastery of the State pattern. First, you will understand the core idea: how encapsulating state behavior in separate classes lets an object change behavior by changing its state object. This matters because it replaces complex conditional logic with clear, testable units. Second, you will implement the pattern in Java: create a context, define a state interface, and write concrete state classes that may change the context’s state. You will practice this with two examples. Third, you will recognize scenarios where State simplifies code, for instance when a class has many conditionals tied to an internal status. Finally, you will compare State with Strategy to avoid confusing them: State often lets state objects trigger transitions and know the context, while Strategy is chosen externally and is usually stateless. Each objective includes a small mnemonic to help you remember why it matters and a verified competency milestone so you can track progress.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Application
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on applying the State pattern in code and evaluating design choices. You will implement concrete state classes that include valid transitions, verify transitions occur through simple tests, and avoid mixing state logic back into the context. Practically, that means writing a Context class that holds a state reference and delegates operations, and state classes that accept the context and call context. setState when a transition should happen. You will also practice writing small unit tests that simulate sequences of actions, asserting the context changes to the expected ConcreteState. Finally, you will practice distinguishing the pattern’s intent by comparing a refactor where behaviors remain in conditionals to the refactor where behaviors move to state classes. These skills help prevent regressions when new states are added and keep each state focused and testable.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Practice & Application

Practice & Application

Hands-on skills you will use to implement and verify State-based designs.

Code
Write a Context that delegates to a state and state classes that call context.setState when appropriate. Keep each state focused.
Checklist
  • State interface with required operations

Test

Example

screens.title: Why conditional logic gets messy
screens.narratorSegment: Start by recognizing the smell. When a class handles many behaviors by testing an internal status and branching in multiple methods, that is the problem State solves. Imagine a TrafficLight implemented with a single class that stores a color string and uses switch statements inside each handler to decide what to do. Every time you add a behavior or a new color you must open that class and modify many branches. That makes the class grow and tests become brittle. The State pattern reassigns responsibility: each behavior lives in a ConcreteState class implementing a shared interface. The Context becomes a thin delegator that simply holds a reference to the current state object. This localization reduces duplication and concentrates transition rules with the code that knows when to change. A common misconception is that State is only useful for UI-like things; in fact it applies anywhere an object's public behavior depends on an underlying mode or status, such as network connections, media players, or vending machines. Example: instead of a switch on color, create RedState, YellowState, GreenState and have the traffic light delegate its request call. That change makes adding a FlashingYellowState trivial and keeps existing states untouched, honoring the Open/Closed Principle. Consider now a class in your codebase that performs many small branches based on the same field — that is the first candidate for refactoring to State.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Conditional Smell
Definition

When conditionals become a maintenance problem

Large classes with repeated switch or if-else blocks that test the same internal field across many methods.
  • The root cause is mixing state representation with state-specific behavior.
  • Adding new states requires modifying many branches, risking regressions.
  • Tests must cover many paths, making refactoring costly.
Analogy
Think of one employee trying to do work for multiple roles in the company by checking which hat they are wearing each day. You would rather have separate role specialists.
Concrete Example
TrafficLight with a color field and switch statements becomes three classes: RedState, YellowState, GreenState to handle requests and transitions.
Key Takeaway

If many methods test the same state, refactor to State to keep behavior localized and extendable.

screens.title: Context, State, ConcreteState
screens.narratorSegment: The State pattern rests on three clear roles. The Context is the object whose behavior varies; it holds a reference to a State and delegates requests to it. The State is an interface or abstract class defining the operations that concrete states implement. ConcreteState classes provide the behavior for each possible state and often know about the Context so they can call context. setState to trigger transitions. This setup means behavior and transitions live with the state implementations rather than being scattered. A common mistake is to make states static or stateless when transitions require context changes; instead, allow states to reference the context or accept it as an argument so they can call the setter and effect transitions. For example, a Door context delegates open, close, lock, and unlock to its current DoorState. ClosedState implements lock by setting the context's state to LockedState. That single line centralizes the transition rule next to the behavior it relates to. The result is a Context that becomes simpler and states that are easy to test in isolation. Remember to keep each state's responsibilities narrow and document any transitions it can perform.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Pattern Structure
Architecture

Context, State, ConcreteState

Each role has a focused responsibility: Context delegates, State defines the interface, ConcreteState implements behavior and transitions.
Context
Holds current state and delegates requests to it.
State
Interface or abstract class that defines operations states must implement.
ConcreteState
Implements behavior and may change the Context's state.
Example: Door
ClosedState.lock calls context.setState(new LockedState()) to perform the transition where the behavior occurs.
<!-- Representative call -->
// Context delegates
public void lock() {
  currentState.lock(this);
}

// In ClosedState
public void lock(Door door) {
  System.out.println("Locking the door.");
  door.setState(new LockedState());
}
Key Takeaway

Put transitions next to the behavior that triggers them so changes are localized and easy to extend.

screens.title: Door example — full Java walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the Door example from the source to see the pattern in action. The DoorState interface defines four methods: open, close, lock, and unlock, each accepting a Door context. ClosedState implements open by printing a message and then calling door. setState(new OpenState()). It implements lock by changing to LockedState. OpenState implements close by changing back to ClosedState and denies locking while open. LockedState denies opening and unlock transitions back to ClosedState. The Door context keeps a reference to the current state and delegates each action to it. This delegation is what removes conditional logic from the context. A common misconception is that this will spread simple logic across many files and make tracing execution harder. In practice, the tracing becomes easier because each state's behavior is small and focused, and you can write tests for each state separately. When you run the Client demo, you will see printed lines indicating the state transitions and the new state's class name. That sequence is a valuable test artifact. When implementing, keep constructors simple and avoid storing long-lived mutable data inside state objects unless it is truly shared state; prefer the context to own shared data.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Door Code Walkthrough
State Interface
interface DoorState {
  void open(Door door);
  void close(Door door);
  void lock(Door door);
  void unlock(Door door);
}

class ClosedState implements DoorState {
  @Override
  public void open(Door door) {
    System.out.println("Opening the door.");
    door.setState(new OpenState());
  }

  @Override
  public void close(Door door) {
    System.out.println("Door is already closed.");
  }

  @Override
  public void lock(Door door) {
    System.out.println("Locking the door.");
    door.setState(new LockedState());
  }

  @Override
  public void unlock(Door door) {
    System.out.println("Door is closed but not locked.");
  }
}
Context: Door
class Door {
  private DoorState currentState;

  public Door() {
    currentState = new ClosedState();
    System.out.println("Door is initially " + currentState.getClass().getSimpleName());
  }

  public void setState(DoorState state) {
    this.currentState = state;
    System.out.println("Door state changed to " + currentState.getClass().getSimpleName());
  }

  public void open() { currentState.open(this); }
  public void close() { currentState.close(this); }
  public void lock() { currentState.lock(this); }
  public void unlock() { currentState.unlock(this); }
}
Check Your Understanding

Why does ClosedState call setState instead of the Door doing the check itself? Think about ownership of transition logic.

screens.title: Refactoring a TrafficLight
screens.narratorSegment: Refactoring a switch-based TrafficLight into the State pattern follows a simple sequence of steps. First, identify the methods that branch on the internal state — for example a handleRequest method that switches over color. Second, define a TrafficLightState interface with the operations used by the Context. Third, create ConcreteState classes for each color, moving the code from the switch cases into the corresponding state class methods. Fourth, modify the TrafficLight context to hold a TrafficLightState reference and delegate calls to it. Finally, ensure transitions occur within state classes by calling context. setState when a different color is the next state. Doing this step-by-step helps preserve behavior while removing branches. A common pitfall is forgetting to move shared helper code out of the old switch into either the context or a shared abstract state. Keep the context responsible for shared data like timers or sensors, and keep the state classes focused on behavior. Example: if the old switch had logging in every case, centralize the logging in the context or a utility method before moving case logic. After refactor, the context becomes much smaller and adding a new FlashingYellowState requires only a new class and perhaps a single registration point.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › TrafficLight Refactor
Steps
  1. Find methods that switch on the state field.
  2. Create a State interface with required operations.
  3. Extract each case into a ConcreteState class.
  4. Change Context to hold a State reference and delegate.
  5. Move transitions into ConcreteState implementations.
Concrete Example
Old: handleRequest switches on color. New: light.handleRequest calls currentState.handleRequest(light). RedState decides to call light.setState(new GreenState()).
Common Mistake

Migrating code piecemeal without centralizing shared helpers leads to duplicated logic. Centralize before extracting.

screens.title: MediaPlayer starter code
screens.narratorSegment: The chapter provides starter code for a MediaPlayer that demonstrates how states change behavior in a small application. The MediaPlayerState interface includes play, pause, stop, and nextSong methods, each accepting the MediaPlayer context. The provided StoppedState includes sensible transitions: play starts playback and switches to PlayingState, nextSong can transition to PlayingState, and pause is invalid while stopped. PlayingState handles pause by switching to PausedState and stop by switching to StoppedState. PausedState resumes to PlayingState on play and also allows stop to transition to StoppedState. When you implement these classes, think about how transitions map to user expectations: pressing next while paused might either queue the next song and remain paused or start playing immediately; the starter code chooses to transition to PlayingState. A useful test sequence is: create a MediaPlayer, call play, call nextSong, call pause, call play, call stop, then call pause to verify the pause call is ignored while stopped. Running this sequence prints state changes and helps you confirm that transitions are implemented exactly as intended. This hands-on task is an excellent way to internalize where transitions belong and how contexts delegate behavior to states.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › MediaPlayer Starter
Starter Code
// MediaPlayerState.java
interface MediaPlayerState {
  void play(MediaPlayer player);
  void pause(MediaPlayer player);
  void stop(MediaPlayer player);
  void nextSong(MediaPlayer player);
}

// StoppedState.java (provided)
class StoppedState implements MediaPlayerState {
  @Override
  public void play(MediaPlayer player) {
    System.out.println("Starting playback from stopped state.");
    player.setState(new PlayingState());
  }
  @Override
  public void pause(MediaPlayer player) {
    System.out.println("Cannot pause, player is stopped.");
  }
  @Override
  public void stop(MediaPlayer player) {
    System.out.println("Player is already stopped.");
  }
  @Override
  public void nextSong(MediaPlayer player) {
    System.out.println("Moving to next song from stopped state.");
    player.setState(new PlayingState());
  }
}
Run Sequence
Simulate the following in main: create player, play, nextSong, pause, play, stop, pause. Expect printed state transitions and one ignored pause while stopped.
Pro Tip

Use small unit tests to simulate the call sequence and assert the class name of current state after each action.

screens.title: State vs Strategy
screens.narratorSegment: State and Strategy share runtime delegation to objects, which often causes confusion. The key difference is intent and ownership. The State pattern changes an object's behavior based on its internal state; state objects often know about the context and drive transitions. The Strategy pattern defines interchangeable algorithms a client or context chooses to use; strategies tend to be stateless and do not call back into the context to change it. For example, a TrafficLight's state classes change the traffic light's behavior and can transition to other states — that is State. A navigation app offering fastest or shortest route choices is Strategy: the app accepts a chosen algorithm and uses it to compute a route, and the algorithm does not typically alter the app's internal selection. A common misconception is to use Strategy when you actually need state transitions; doing so pushes transition logic into the context and recreates complex conditional code. When deciding, ask whether the behavior depends on an internal mode that will cause the object to transition on its own; if so, State is usually the better choice.

keyIdea.title: Decision Rule
keyIdea.text: If behavior is driven by internal mode and requires transitions, prefer State; if you need interchangeable algorithms chosen externally, prefer Strategy.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › State vs Strategy
State
Object changes behavior based on internal state. State objects often know the context and can change it.
  • Context holds current state
  • Transitions happen inside states
  • Useful for mode-driven behavior
Strategy
Context or client selects an algorithm. Strategies are interchangeable and typically stateless.
  • Client chooses a strategy
  • Strategies don't change context
  • Useful for algorithm selection
Analogy
State: a traffic light that moves through modes on its own. Strategy: a driver choosing the navigation method before starting a trip.
Key Takeaway

Ask who chooses and who drives transitions: external selection suggests Strategy; internal transitions suggest State.

screens.title: Pitfalls and misconceptions
screens.narratorSegment: There are several recurring mistakes when applying the State pattern. First, treating State as a pure replacement for Strategy without considering transitions. If you extract behaviors but keep the context driving transitions, you have not gained the full benefit. Second, giving state objects too much shared mutable data. State objects should be small and focused; shared data belongs on the context. Third, prematurely extracting states when a class only needs a tiny variation — refactoring is worthwhile when the branching is across many methods or when behavior grows. Fourth, scattering helper logic across states instead of centralizing common operations can lead to duplication. To avoid these traps, identify the ownership of data and transitions before extracting states, keep state classes focused, and write tests for each state to protect behavior during future changes. Finally, document transitions: a simple comment listing valid next states per ConcreteState helps future maintainers understand allowed flows. These practices keep the pattern maintainable and predictable. Pitfalls and misconceptions means don't confuse state with strategy, don't put shared mutable data in states, and centralize common helpers to avoid duplication.. In practical terms, what learners often get wrong and how to avoid it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Testing stateful objects
screens.narratorSegment: Testing State-based designs is straightforward because each state encapsulates behavior. Write unit tests for each ConcreteState in isolation by constructing a mock or real Context and calling the state methods directly, asserting expected transitions via the Context's current state class name or a test hook. Also write integration-style tests that exercise sequences through the Context's public A P I, such as play, next, pause in a MediaPlayer, and assert the Context ends up in the expected state. When debugging, print statements showing the class name of the new state are very helpful; for example, context. setState(new PlayingState()) followed by a log of currentState. getClass(). getSimpleName. A common misunderstanding is that tests must replicate the old conditional structure; instead, focus on observable behavior and state transitions. Use small helper assertions such as assertTrue(currentState instanceof PlayingState) or assertEquals("PlayingState", currentState. getClass(). getSimpleName()). Finally, test invalid actions locally: calling pause while stopped should result in no transition and possibly an error message. These checks confirm that each state enforces valid behavior and that transitions are only possible where intended. Testing stateful objects means unit-test states individually and write sequence tests for the context to ensure transitions and invalid actions behave as intended.. In practical terms, write tests that assert behavior and transitions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: When to use State in real projects
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding to apply the State pattern depends on maintainability goals. Use State when an object exhibits distinct modes where many methods branch on the same internal field and when transitions are meaningful behaviors that should be expressible in code. It’s especially helpful for systems with clear lifecycle phases, such as media players, UI controls, network connections, or vending machines. When using State, keep these practices in mind: centralize shared data in the Context, keep state classes small and focused, place transitions in the state methods, and document valid next states for each ConcreteState to help maintainers. Avoid overengineering: if you only have one or two simple branches and behavior is unlikely to grow, the added indirection may not be worth it. Finally, prefer composition over inheritance for states so that adding a new state is as simple as adding a new class without touching existing ones. Regularly run your unit tests when refactoring to State to prevent hidden regressions. These patterns keep your code clear and enable safe extension as requirements evolve. screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Here are three compact ideas to carry forward. First, the State pattern lets an object alter its behavior by swapping state objects; transitions and behavior live together in ConcreteState implementations. Second, the pattern improves maintainability by removing central switch or if-else logic and adhering to the Open/Closed Principle: new states are added by adding classes, not changing existing ones. Third, State differs from Strategy in intent: State manages behavior based on internal mode and often allows state objects to change the context; Strategy is an externally chosen algorithm that is typically stateless. Keep these concepts in mind as you refactor conditional logic, design lifecycles, and test stateful interactions. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we explore the State pattern and why it matters. Many objects change how they behave depending on internal conditions, and code that keeps checking those conditions quickly becomes brittle and hard to extend. The State pattern solves that by moving each state’s behavior into its own class. You’ll learn the three core parts — a Context that delegates behavior, a State interface defining the contract, and ConcreteState implementations that encapsulate behavior and transitions. We will see concrete Java examples such as a traffic light and a door, and you will practice implementing a MediaPlayer with Playing, Paused, and Stopped states. By the end you should be able to recognize when a large switch or many if-else branches really mean an opportunity for State, and you will be able to refactor to make code easier to extend without changing existing classes. Notice too how the State pattern differs from Strategy: State objects often drive transitions and know the context, while strategies are chosen externally and are usually stateless. Think about a traffic light changing from red to green as an object that appears to change its class, and ask yourself where you still rely on conditional switches in your own code.

By the end of this chapter you will do four concrete tasks that show mastery of the State pattern. First, you will understand the core idea: how encapsulating state behavior in separate classes lets an object change behavior by changing its state object. This matters because it replaces complex conditional logic with clear, testable units. Second, you will implement the pattern in Java: create a context, define a state interface, and write concrete state classes that may change the context’s state. You will practice this with two examples. Third, you will recognize scenarios where State simplifies code, for instance when a class has many conditionals tied to an internal status. Finally, you will compare State with Strategy to avoid confusing them: State often lets state objects trigger transitions and know the context, while Strategy is chosen externally and is usually stateless. Each objective includes a small mnemonic to help you remember why it matters and a verified competency milestone so you can track progress.

This second objectives slide focuses on applying the State pattern in code and evaluating design choices. You will implement concrete state classes that include valid transitions, verify transitions occur through simple tests, and avoid mixing state logic back into the context. Practically, that means writing a Context class that holds a state reference and delegates operations, and state classes that accept the context and call context. setState when a transition should happen. You will also practice writing small unit tests that simulate sequences of actions, asserting the context changes to the expected ConcreteState. Finally, you will practice distinguishing the pattern’s intent by comparing a refactor where behaviors remain in conditionals to the refactor where behaviors move to state classes. These skills help prevent regressions when new states are added and keep each state focused and testable.

Start by recognizing the smell. When a class handles many behaviors by testing an internal status and branching in multiple methods, that is the problem State solves. Imagine a TrafficLight implemented with a single class that stores a color string and uses switch statements inside each handler to decide what to do. Every time you add a behavior or a new color you must open that class and modify many branches. That makes the class grow and tests become brittle. The State pattern reassigns responsibility: each behavior lives in a ConcreteState class implementing a shared interface. The Context becomes a thin delegator that simply holds a reference to the current state object. This localization reduces duplication and concentrates transition rules with the code that knows when to change. A common misconception is that State is only useful for UI-like things; in fact it applies anywhere an object's public behavior depends on an underlying mode or status, such as network connections, media players, or vending machines. Example: instead of a switch on color, create RedState, YellowState, GreenState and have the traffic light delegate its request call. That change makes adding a FlashingYellowState trivial and keeps existing states untouched, honoring the Open/Closed Principle. Consider now a class in your codebase that performs many small branches based on the same field — that is the first candidate for refactoring to State.

The State pattern rests on three clear roles. The Context is the object whose behavior varies; it holds a reference to a State and delegates requests to it. The State is an interface or abstract class defining the operations that concrete states implement. ConcreteState classes provide the behavior for each possible state and often know about the Context so they can call context. setState to trigger transitions. This setup means behavior and transitions live with the state implementations rather than being scattered. A common mistake is to make states static or stateless when transitions require context changes; instead, allow states to reference the context or accept it as an argument so they can call the setter and effect transitions. For example, a Door context delegates open, close, lock, and unlock to its current DoorState. ClosedState implements lock by setting the context's state to LockedState. That single line centralizes the transition rule next to the behavior it relates to. The result is a Context that becomes simpler and states that are easy to test in isolation. Remember to keep each state's responsibilities narrow and document any transitions it can perform.

Let's walk through the Door example from the source to see the pattern in action. The DoorState interface defines four methods: open, close, lock, and unlock, each accepting a Door context. ClosedState implements open by printing a message and then calling door. setState(new OpenState()). It implements lock by changing to LockedState. OpenState implements close by changing back to ClosedState and denies locking while open. LockedState denies opening and unlock transitions back to ClosedState. The Door context keeps a reference to the current state and delegates each action to it. This delegation is what removes conditional logic from the context. A common misconception is that this will spread simple logic across many files and make tracing execution harder. In practice, the tracing becomes easier because each state's behavior is small and focused, and you can write tests for each state separately. When you run the Client demo, you will see printed lines indicating the state transitions and the new state's class name. That sequence is a valuable test artifact. When implementing, keep constructors simple and avoid storing long-lived mutable data inside state objects unless it is truly shared state; prefer the context to own shared data.

Refactoring a switch-based TrafficLight into the State pattern follows a simple sequence of steps. First, identify the methods that branch on the internal state — for example a handleRequest method that switches over color. Second, define a TrafficLightState interface with the operations used by the Context. Third, create ConcreteState classes for each color, moving the code from the switch cases into the corresponding state class methods. Fourth, modify the TrafficLight context to hold a TrafficLightState reference and delegate calls to it. Finally, ensure transitions occur within state classes by calling context. setState when a different color is the next state. Doing this step-by-step helps preserve behavior while removing branches. A common pitfall is forgetting to move shared helper code out of the old switch into either the context or a shared abstract state. Keep the context responsible for shared data like timers or sensors, and keep the state classes focused on behavior. Example: if the old switch had logging in every case, centralize the logging in the context or a utility method before moving case logic. After refactor, the context becomes much smaller and adding a new FlashingYellowState requires only a new class and perhaps a single registration point.

The chapter provides starter code for a MediaPlayer that demonstrates how states change behavior in a small application. The MediaPlayerState interface includes play, pause, stop, and nextSong methods, each accepting the MediaPlayer context. The provided StoppedState includes sensible transitions: play starts playback and switches to PlayingState, nextSong can transition to PlayingState, and pause is invalid while stopped. PlayingState handles pause by switching to PausedState and stop by switching to StoppedState. PausedState resumes to PlayingState on play and also allows stop to transition to StoppedState. When you implement these classes, think about how transitions map to user expectations: pressing next while paused might either queue the next song and remain paused or start playing immediately; the starter code chooses to transition to PlayingState. A useful test sequence is: create a MediaPlayer, call play, call nextSong, call pause, call play, call stop, then call pause to verify the pause call is ignored while stopped. Running this sequence prints state changes and helps you confirm that transitions are implemented exactly as intended. This hands-on task is an excellent way to internalize where transitions belong and how contexts delegate behavior to states.

State and Strategy share runtime delegation to objects, which often causes confusion. The key difference is intent and ownership. The State pattern changes an object's behavior based on its internal state; state objects often know about the context and drive transitions. The Strategy pattern defines interchangeable algorithms a client or context chooses to use; strategies tend to be stateless and do not call back into the context to change it. For example, a TrafficLight's state classes change the traffic light's behavior and can transition to other states — that is State. A navigation app offering fastest or shortest route choices is Strategy: the app accepts a chosen algorithm and uses it to compute a route, and the algorithm does not typically alter the app's internal selection. A common misconception is to use Strategy when you actually need state transitions; doing so pushes transition logic into the context and recreates complex conditional code. When deciding, ask whether the behavior depends on an internal mode that will cause the object to transition on its own; if so, State is usually the better choice.

There are several recurring mistakes when applying the State pattern. First, treating State as a pure replacement for Strategy without considering transitions. If you extract behaviors but keep the context driving transitions, you have not gained the full benefit. Second, giving state objects too much shared mutable data. State objects should be small and focused; shared data belongs on the context. Third, prematurely extracting states when a class only needs a tiny variation — refactoring is worthwhile when the branching is across many methods or when behavior grows. Fourth, scattering helper logic across states instead of centralizing common operations can lead to duplication. To avoid these traps, identify the ownership of data and transitions before extracting states, keep state classes focused, and write tests for each state to protect behavior during future changes. Finally, document transitions: a simple comment listing valid next states per ConcreteState helps future maintainers understand allowed flows. These practices keep the pattern maintainable and predictable. Pitfalls and misconceptions means don't confuse state with strategy, don't put shared mutable data in states, and centralize common helpers to avoid duplication.. In practical terms, what learners often get wrong and how to avoid it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Testing State-based designs is straightforward because each state encapsulates behavior. Write unit tests for each ConcreteState in isolation by constructing a mock or real Context and calling the state methods directly, asserting expected transitions via the Context's current state class name or a test hook. Also write integration-style tests that exercise sequences through the Context's public A P I, such as play, next, pause in a MediaPlayer, and assert the Context ends up in the expected state. When debugging, print statements showing the class name of the new state are very helpful; for example, context. setState(new PlayingState()) followed by a log of currentState. getClass(). getSimpleName. A common misunderstanding is that tests must replicate the old conditional structure; instead, focus on observable behavior and state transitions. Use small helper assertions such as assertTrue(currentState instanceof PlayingState) or assertEquals("PlayingState", currentState. getClass(). getSimpleName()). Finally, test invalid actions locally: calling pause while stopped should result in no transition and possibly an error message. These checks confirm that each state enforces valid behavior and that transitions are only possible where intended. Deciding to apply the State pattern depends on maintainability goals. Use State when an object exhibits distinct modes where many methods branch on the same internal field and when transitions are meaningful behaviors that should be expressible in code. It’s especially helpful for systems with clear lifecycle phases, such as media players, UI controls, network connections, or vending machines. When using State, keep these practices in mind: centralize shared data in the Context, keep state classes small and focused, place transitions in the state methods, and document valid next states for each ConcreteState to help maintainers. Avoid overengineering: if you only have one or two simple branches and behavior is unlikely to grow, the added indirection may not be worth it. Finally, prefer composition over inheritance for states so that adding a new state is as simple as adding a new class without touching existing ones. Regularly run your unit tests when refactoring to State to prevent hidden regressions. These patterns keep your code clear and enable safe extension as requirements evolve. Here are three compact ideas to carry forward. First, the State pattern lets an object alter its behavior by swapping state objects; transitions and behavior live together in ConcreteState implementations. Second, the pattern improves maintainability by removing central switch or if-else logic and adhering to the Open/Closed Principle: new states are added by adding classes, not changing existing ones. Third, State differs from Strategy in intent: State manages behavior based on internal mode and often allows state objects to change the context; Strategy is an externally chosen algorithm that is typically stateless. Keep these concepts in mind as you refactor conditional logic, design lifecycles, and test stateful interactions. A final quick review to anchor learning. First, localize behavior: when methods branch on the same internal property, move those branches into state classes. Second, test transitions: each ConcreteState should have unit tests that assert valid transitions and that invalid actions don't change state. Third, choose the pattern intentionally: pick State when the object itself needs to change mode and manage transitions; pick Strategy when you need interchangeable algorithms provided by the client.
